title: The Registry Office and the Cell: Sardinia, the Factory Councils, and Thirty-Three Notebooks
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Registry Office and the Fall

stops.name: Ales, the fourth child
stops.date_confidence: attested; International Gramsci Society chronology and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy agree on 22 January 1891 at Ales. Coordinates corrected to the town's own position, 39.767 N 8.817 E; the incoming research gave two different and both wrong pairs. The mother's surname appears as Marcias in English sources and Marcia in some Italian ones.
stops.campa: In the hill town of Ales, in the province of Cagliari, Giuseppina Marcias bears her fourth child on the twenty-second of January. They register him as Antonio Francesco Gramsci. The island is one generation into unification and has not yet been paid for it. His father Francesco holds a post in the registry service, one of the small salaried offices by which the Italian state reaches into Sardinian villages, and the household lives on that wage. There will be seven children in all, four sons and three daughters.
suggested_refs: The parish and civil birth registers of Ales, January 1891
sources: International Gramsci Society, Chronology of Antonio Gramsci's Life

stops.name: Sorgono, the eighteenth month
stops.date_confidence: attested as to cause and place, reconstructed as to month. Italian Wikipedia gives Pott's disease contracted at about eighteen months at Sorgono, which puts it in mid-1892; the day is unknown and 1 July orders the segment. The rival account of a fall is biographical tradition traceable to Giuseppe Fiori's Vita di Antonio Gramsci (1966), not fetched this pass.
stops.campa: The family follows Francesco's posting to the registry office at Sorgono, in the mountains of the Barbagia, and stays seven years. At about eighteen months the boy contracts Pott's disease, tuberculosis of the spine. The household treats it with the remedies of the village rather than with doctors. The vertebrae collapse. He will never grow past four foot eleven and will carry a curved back and a constant low pain for the rest of his life. A rival account, repeated by his biographers, says he was dropped by a servant and fell down a flight of stairs.
suggested_refs: Giuseppe Fiori, Vita di Antonio Gramsci (1966), source of the fall tradition

stops.name: Ghilarza, the father taken
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the IGS chronology places the suspension and arrest under 1898, correcting a widely repeated 1897. The day is unknown and 1 January orders the segment. Trial verdict of 27 October 1900 and the sentence length come from Italian Wikipedia. Coordinates are the surveyed position of Casa Gramsci, Corso Umberto I 57.
stops.campa: An inspection of the Sorgono registry office ends Francesco Gramsci's career. He is suspended, arrested, and charged with peculato, concussione and falsity in acts; the trial closes on the twenty-seventh of October 1900 with a sentence of five years, eight months and twenty-two days. The state that employed the father now holds him. Giuseppina moves the children to Ghilarza, to the house on Corso Umberto I, and holds them together on sewing work and on what relatives in the village will give her.
suggested_refs: The house at Corso Umberto I 57, Ghilarza, today the Casa Museo Antonio Gramsci

stops.name: Ghilarza, the boy at the tax agency
stops.date_confidence: attested; casamuseogramsci.it states he worked two years at the Agenzia delle Imposte dirette e del Catasto at Ghilarza because of the family's poverty, and the IGS chronology places the employment in 1903-1905. The day is unknown. The wage figure and the detail of the registers' weight come from the Fiori biography and are tradition, not fetched.
stops.campa: There is not enough money to keep every child in school at once, so Antonio is taken out of it. For two years he works at the Agenzia delle Imposte dirette e del Catasto in Ghilarza, ten hours a day for nine lire a month, carrying the ledgers of land and tax from shelf to desk. When the money allows he is sent back to school, two years behind the boys of his age. He reads whatever comes into the house. Fiori's biography adds that the registers weighed more than the boy who carried them.
suggested_refs: The land and tax registers of the Ghilarza cadastral office, c. 1903-1905
sources: Giuseppe Fiori, Vita di Antonio Gramsci (1966)

stops.name: Santu Lussurgiu, the ginnasio
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1905-1908 by Italian Wikipedia and the IGS chronology; 1906 is a midpoint chosen to order the segment. Coordinates corrected: the incoming longitude of 8.75 sat about 8.5 km east of the town. The description of three teachers covering the whole curriculum is standard in the biographies and was not fetched this pass.
stops.campa: He boards at the ginnasio in Santu Lussurgiu, a school where three teachers cover the whole five-year curriculum, and lodges cheaply and badly, away from his mother for the first time. He is the smallest boy in the school, and among the poorest, and his back and his health set him apart again. Here he begins reading the socialist press that reaches Sardinia late and secondhand, and writing to his brother Gennaro about it. He sits the closing examinations at Oristano in 1908 and passes them.
suggested_refs: The ginnasio of Santu Lussurgiu; the examination board at Oristano, 1908

stops.name: Cagliari, the Liceo Dettori and his brother's Avanti!
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1908-1911; October 1908 orders the segment. The IGS chronology tags the cluster of first article and graduation as reconstruction rather than firm attestation. Coordinates are central Cagliari: the exact position of the liceo building was not located, so this is a town-level pin, not a landmark one.
stops.campa: At the Liceo Dettori in Cagliari he lodges with his older brother Gennaro, back from military service on the mainland a socialist, who brings copies of Avanti! into the room. Sardinia is arguing with itself about autonomy, about the tariff that ruins its shepherds, about whether the island is a colony of Turin and Milan. Gramsci at seventeen is a Sardinian nationalist before he is anything else. His first published article appears in L'Unione Sarda in 1910. He graduates in the summer of 1911 and applies for a scholarship.
suggested_refs: Gramsci's earliest signed piece in L'Unione Sarda, Cagliari, 1910

stops.name: Turin, the Collegio Carlo Alberto examination
stops.date_confidence: attested; the IGS chronology gives the scholarship in October 1911 and enrolment in Letters in November 1911. The ninth-place ranking, the count of thirty-nine places and the seventy-lire stipend are standard in the biographies and were not verified against a fetched source. Coordinates are central Turin: the college's own address was not confirmed.
stops.campa: He sits the competitive examination of the Collegio Carlo Alberto, which offers thirty-nine places to poor students of the old Kingdom of Sardinia, and places ninth. Another candidate that year, from Genoa, is Palmiro Togliatti. In November he crosses to the mainland and enrolls in Letters at the University of Turin, a city of half a million with the largest concentrated industrial workforce in Italy, and a winter his Sardinian body has no defence against. The scholarship pays seventy lire a month. He is often cold and often hungry.
suggested_refs: The Collegio Carlo Alberto scholarship rolls for the academic year 1911-12

stops.name: Turin, Bartoli's student
stops.date_confidence: attested for the study under Matteo Bartoli and the friendship with Togliatti from 1912, per the Stanford Encyclopedia and the IGS chronology; the day is arbitrary. Bartoli's remark about the neogrammarians is biographical tradition, not a fetched quotation. Coordinates estimate the historic faculty buildings on Via Po.
stops.campa: He studies under Matteo Bartoli, who teaches linguistics as the study of how forms spread and displace one another, which speech prevails over which and by what means, and who tells colleagues that this Sardinian will be the one to overturn the neogrammarians. Gramsci works on the dialects of his own island. He shares lodgings and a poverty with other scholarship students, Togliatti and Angelo Tasca among them, and reads Croce, whose idealism he will spend twenty years arguing with. He is nineteen and coughing.
suggested_refs: Matteo Bartoli's neolinguistic teaching at Turin, and Gramsci's unfinished work on Sardinian dialect

stops.name: Turin, the party card
stops.date_confidence: disputed, and the file does not resolve it. The IGS chronology hedges, 'Probably, Gramsci became a member of the Socialist Party in Turin during this period', following October 1913. Italian Wikipedia gives 1914 on Togliatti's recollection. Gramsci never recorded the date himself. 1 October 1913 is used only to order the segment.
stops.campa: He joins the Italian Socialist Party in Turin. The section he enters is the largest and most industrial in Italy. In the same period the elections of 1913, the first held under near-universal male suffrage, empty the Sardinian countryside into a national ballot, and the peasant question and the factory question begin to look to him like one question. The date of the card itself is the thing nobody can fix: Togliatti remembered 1914, the party's own chronology places it somewhere after October 1913, and Gramsci never wrote it down.
suggested_refs: The membership rolls of the Turin section of the PSI, 1913-1914

stops.name: Turin, the last examination
stops.date_confidence: attested; the IGS chronology and Britannica both give 12 April 1915 as the final examination and record that he never graduated. The Stanford Encyclopedia dates the first Grido del Popolo contributions to 1914 and the Avanti! staff appointment to December 1915. Coordinates are central Turin: the newspaper's office address was not located.
stops.campa: On the twelfth of April he sits an examination in the Faculty of Letters. It is the last one he will ever sit. He does not withdraw from the university so much as stop returning to it. Italy enters the war the following month, and he is exempt on grounds of health, so the war years are spent in a newspaper office. He joins the editorial staff of the Piedmont edition of Avanti!, writing political comment and theatre criticism, much of it unsigned, for a wage he can live on.
suggested_refs: Gramsci's unsigned theatre criticism in the Piedmont edition of Avanti!, 1916-1920

stops.name: Turin, La Citta Futura, one issue
stops.date_confidence: attested; the IGS chronology dates the single issue to 11 February 1917 and the election as secretary of the Turin PSI section to September 1917. The August 1917 rising and the wholesale arrest of the Turin leadership are standard chronology corroborated across the sources consulted.
stops.campa: He fills a single number of a review called La Citta Futura, a one-off issue of the Piedmont socialist youth federation, writing most of it himself: on indifference, on discipline, on the duty of the young to prepare themselves before the moment arrives rather than after it. The issue is dated the eleventh of February 1917. There is no second. Six months later a bread riot in Turin turns into four days of street fighting and the party's Turin leadership is arrested wholesale; in September the section elects Gramsci its secretary.
suggested_refs: La Citta Futura, single issue, 11 February 1917, Piedmont socialist youth federation

stops.name: Turin, the revolution against Capital
stops.date_confidence: disputed as to date and printed here unresolved. The IGS chronology and the marxists.org translation header give 24 December 1917 in the national edition of Avanti!; Italian Wikipedia gives 24 November 1917. The December date orders the segment. The quotation is verbatim from the marxists.org translation.
stops.campa: Petrograd has been in Bolshevik hands for six weeks when Gramsci publishes the essay in Avanti! Karl Marx's book had taught, as its Italian readers understood it, that Russia must pass through a full capitalism before it could pass beyond one, and Lenin's revolution has refused the schedule. Gramsci does not treat this as an embarrassment to be explained away. He treats it as the point. Italian sources date the article the twenty-fourth of November; the international chronology says the twenty-fourth of December.
stops.quote: It is the revolution against Karl Marx's Capital.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Gramsci, 'The Revolution Against Capital', Avanti!, 1917, Marxists Internet Archive translation
suggested_refs: The text of 'La rivoluzione contro il Capitale' in the national edition of Avanti!, late 1917
sources: Marxists Internet Archive, 'The Revolution Against Capital'

stops.name: Turin, the first issue of L'Ordine Nuovo
stops.date_confidence: attested; the IGS chronology dates the inaugural issue to 1 May 1919 and names Tasca, Terracini and Togliatti as co-founders. The quotation is from Gramsci's own retrospective account of 1921, written about this period rather than during it. Coordinates are central Turin: the editorial office's street address was not located.
stops.campa: With Angelo Tasca, Umberto Terracini and Palmiro Togliatti he brings out the first number of L'Ordine Nuovo on the first of May, four socialists in their twenties running a weekly review of socialist culture out of Turin. Within weeks Gramsci turns it away from culture and toward the internal commissions of the metal shops, the elected shop committees that already exist inside the factories, and reads them as something nobody has yet named: the organs of a state the workers are building without permission, inside the one they live under.
stops.quote: For the first time in history, there was an example of a proletariat which engaged in struggle for the control of production, without having been forced into action by hunger or unemployment.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Gramsci, 'The Turin Factory Council Movement', 1921, Marxists Internet Archive translation
suggested_refs: The complete run of L'Ordine Nuovo, Turin, 1919-1920
sources: Marxists Internet Archive, 'The Turin Factory Council Movement'

stops.name: Turin, workers' democracy
stops.date_confidence: attested; the article ran in L'Ordine Nuovo on 21 June 1919 and the quotation is verbatim from the marxists.org translation. The July arrest during a political strike is attested by the IGS chronology, which does not give the day.
stops.campa: The June article, written with Togliatti, asks how to control the immense social forces which the war has unleashed, and answers by pointing at what already exists. Turn the internal commissions into councils elected by every worker in the shop, organized and unorganized alike, and the machinery of a workers' state is standing before the revolution rather than after it. In July, during a political strike called against the Allied intervention in Russia, he is arrested. The councils spread through the Turin metal industry that autumn.
stops.quote: The socialist state potentially already exists in the institutions of social life characteristic of the exploited working class.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Gramsci, 'Workers' Democracy', L'Ordine Nuovo, 21 June 1919, Marxists Internet Archive translation
suggested_refs: 'Democrazia operaia', L'Ordine Nuovo, 21 June 1919

stops.name: Turin, the metal shops and the general strike
stops.date_confidence: attested; the IGS chronology gives the lockout of 27-28 March 1920, the general strike of over 200,000 workers on 13 April, and the defeat by 24 April. Coordinates approximate Turin's early-twentieth-century industrial district rather than any single plant: Lingotto only partly overlaps these events and Mirafiori postdates them by two decades. The influence of Sorel is scholarly consensus rather than a documented Gramsci statement of this date.
stops.campa: The industrialists lock the metal shops on the twenty-seventh of March; on the thirteenth of April more than two hundred thousand workers are out in Turin and the province. No other Italian city moves. Gramsci had read Georges Sorel on the general strike as a myth that makes a class act, and what Turin shows him is a class acting alone, in one city, against a state that can afford to wait. The general confederation and the party's own leadership do nothing. By the twenty-fourth the strike is over and the councils are broken.
stops.quote: The Turin proletariat was however isolated from the rest of Italy; the central organs did nothing to help it.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Gramsci, 'The Turin Factory Council Movement', 1921, Marxists Internet Archive translation
suggested_refs: Georges Sorel, Reflexions sur la violence, read by the Ordine Nuovo group at Turin
sources: Marxists Internet Archive, 'The Turin Factory Council Movement'

stops.name: Livorno, the Teatro Goldoni
stops.date_confidence: attested; the congress ran 15-21 January 1921 at the Teatro Goldoni, Via Goldoni 83, whose published position supplies the coordinates. The vote figures are rounded here from the widely reported totals and were not verified against a congress record this pass.
stops.campa: The Seventeenth Congress of the Italian Socialist Party opens in the Teatro Goldoni on the fifteenth of January. Moscow has made twenty-one conditions of admission to the Communist International, the twenty-first of which requires the expulsion of the reformists. The maximalist majority around Serrati will not expel them. Three days of speeches change no one's arithmetic. The motions are counted: about fifty-eight thousand mandates for the communist motion, about ninety-eight thousand against it.
suggested_refs: The twenty-one conditions of admission to the Communist International, 1920

stops.name: Livorno, the Teatro San Marco
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Communist Party of Italy was founded at the Teatro San Marco on 21 January 1921. Coordinates corrected to the theatre's own published position on Via San Marco, replacing a guessed pin about 750 m away. The umbrella detail is stated by the same source.
stops.campa: On the morning of the twenty-first the communist minority walks out of the Goldoni and across Livorno to the Teatro San Marco. There they constitute the Partito Comunista d'Italia, sezione italiana dell'Internazionale Comunista. Amadeo Bordiga's abstentionist current dominates the new party's leadership, and Gramsci, who argued for the split and has got it, is a minority inside it and will stay one for three years. The hall is in such disrepair that the delegates sit through the founding session under open umbrellas.
suggested_refs: The Teatro San Marco, Via San Marco, Livorno, founding hall of the PCd'I

stops.name: Moscow, the delegate arrives
stops.date_confidence: attested; the IGS chronology gives departure on 26 May 1922 with Graziadei and Bordiga and arrival via Latvia on 23 June 1922. The route through Berlin is standard in the biographies but was not fetched. The coordinate is the Mokhovaya Street area, where a commemorative plaque records that he worked; the plaque's installation date is not given by any source reached.
stops.campa: Sent as the party's delegate to the Communist International, he leaves Italy on the twenty-sixth of May with Bordiga and Antonio Graziadei, travels by way of Berlin and Riga, and reaches Moscow on the twenty-third of June, a month on the road. He is thirty-one and arriving in a country that has just come through famine. He works from an office on Mokhovaya Street. He is also, by the time he arrives, ill enough that the International sends him out of the city almost at once.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at Mokhovaya Street 16, Moscow, naming Gramsci a founder of the Italian Communist Party

stops.name: Serebryany Bor, the sanatorium
stops.date_confidence: attested as to place and meeting; the IGS chronology states that he went to recuperate at the Serebranyi Bor sanatorium and that he met Julia Schucht during the stay. The exact day is unknown and 30 June orders the segment. Coordinates corrected to the district's own position, about 2.8 km from the pin given in the incoming research.
stops.campa: At the sanatorium in the pine woods of Serebryany Bor, on the river loop north-west of Moscow, he is set among convalescing Bolsheviks and foreign delegates and told to rest. There he meets the Schucht sisters, Eugenia first and then Giulia, daughters of an exiled Russian family raised partly in Italy. They marry, and two sons follow, Delio in 1924 and Giuliano in 1926. Of the fifteen years the marriage will last he will spend fewer than three in the same country as his wife. Giulia plays the violin.
suggested_refs: The Serebryany Bor sanatorium, Moscow, where Gramsci met Giulia Schucht

stops.name: Vienna, the foreign bureau
stops.date_confidence: attested; the IGS chronology gives the February 1923 round-up and warrant, the November assignment, and arrival on 3 December 1923. l'Unita's founding on 12 February 1924 is attested, and it was printed initially at Milan, not Rome as some accounts have it; Gramsci did not travel to Milan for it, so the founding is recorded here, where he was. Coordinates are central Vienna: no street address was located. The quotation is Gramsci's own phrase as given by Italian Wikipedia.
stops.campa: A February round-up takes the party's leadership in Italy and a warrant is issued in his name. He stays out. The International posts him to Vienna, where he arrives on the third of December to run the foreign bureau of a party that no longer has a legal existence at home. He argues by letter for two things his own leadership resists: a united front against fascism, and a newspaper that would bind the northern workers to the peasants of the south. The paper appears at Milan on the twelfth of February 1924, and he gives it its name, l'Unita.
stops.quote: una stanza fredda e inospitale della capitale austriaca
stops.quote_source: Antonio Gramsci on his Vienna lodging, quoted in Italian Wikipedia, 'Antonio Gramsci'
suggested_refs: The first number of l'Unita, Milan, 12 February 1924

stops.name: Rome, the return under immunity
stops.date_confidence: attested with a minor unresolved variance: the IGS chronology gives election in absentia on 6 April 1924 and return to Italy on 12 May 1924, while English Wikipedia gives 24 May for the election. Coordinates inherit the canonical Rome pin already used across the corpus.
stops.campa: Elected in absentia for the Veneto on the sixth of April, he crosses back into Italy on the twelfth of May after nearly two years abroad, protected by nothing but the immunity of a deputy in a chamber the government is already dismantling. He takes rooms in Rome and begins the work of turning a party built by Bordiga for insurrection into one that can survive underground for as long as the regime lasts, which he does not expect to be a short time. Giulia stays in Moscow with the child she is carrying.
suggested_refs: The Veneto constituency returns of the April 1924 general election

stops.name: Rome, general secretary
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date. Britannica gives 'Summer 1924' for the general secretaryship and the IGS chronology pins no day; 15 August orders the segment. Delio's birth in Moscow on 10 August 1924 is attested by IGS; Gramsci was in Italy, so it is recorded here as news reaching him rather than staged as a Moscow scene. The Aventine dispute is attested in the chronology.
stops.campa: In August the party makes him its general secretary. The Matteotti murder in June has emptied the Chamber, most of the opposition having walked out to the Aventine in protest, and Gramsci takes the communist deputies back onto the benches instead, arguing that a boycott of the only public floor left standing is a gift to the man standing on it. The other opposition parties never forgive the decision. In the same month, in Moscow, Giulia gives birth to their first son, Delio; the news reaches him by letter.
suggested_refs: The Aventine Secession of June 1924 and the PCd'I's refusal to join it

stops.name: Rome, Montecitorio, the only speech
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date, subject and outcome. Coordinates inherit the Chamber of Deputies pin already in use in mussolini.journey.json. The transcript at marxists.org is a paraphrase-adjacent English rendering rather than a certified verbatim record, so nothing is quoted from it here; the detail of Mussolini's repeated interruptions comes from that framing and is not a stenographic finding.
stops.campa: He rises in the Chamber on the sixteenth of May to speak against a bill outlawing secret associations, aimed at Freemasonry, and tells the deputies what the law is actually for: not the lodges, which the regime can absorb, but every form of organization it does not control, which it will now be able to dissolve by decree. Mussolini interrupts him repeatedly from the government bench. It is the only major speech Gramsci makes in the four years he holds a seat, and the bill passes.
suggested_refs: Marxists Internet Archive transcript of the speech to the Chamber of Deputies, 16 May 1925
sources: Marxists Internet Archive, speech of 16 May 1925

stops.name: Lyon, the clandestine congress
stops.date_confidence: attested; the IGS chronology and Britannica give the Third Congress at Lyon, 20-26 January 1926, with Gramsci's theses taking 90.8 per cent. Coordinates are central Lyon: no source reached identified the building the congress met in, which is a genuine gap.
stops.campa: The Third Congress of the party meets clandestinely at Lyon, chosen for the size of its Italian emigrant colony, delegates crossing the border on false papers to attend. The theses Gramsci drafts with Togliatti carry ninety point eight per cent of the vote and settle the party's line: fascism is not a passing reaction of a frightened bourgeoisie but a regime with a social base of its own, and it will be beaten only by an alliance between the workers of the north and the peasants of the south.
suggested_refs: The Lyon Theses of January 1926, drafted by Gramsci and Togliatti

stops.name: Rome, the letter to Moscow
stops.date_confidence: attested as to content and month; the IGS chronology and the marxists.org text place the Political Bureau letter in October 1926 and record Togliatti's refusal to transmit it as intended. The exact day is not given by the sources reached and 14 October orders the segment. Coordinates inherit the canonical Rome pin; the drafting location within the city is not specified.
stops.campa: He drafts a letter from the party's political bureau to the central committee of the Soviet party. It backs the majority against Leon Trotsky, Zinoviev and Kamenev, and then says the thing that will keep it from being delivered: that a victory won by crushing a minority would cost the Soviet leadership the moral authority on which the whole International rests. The two men argue about it by post, and the argument is unfinished when the police come. Togliatti, in Moscow, reads the letter and does not pass it on as it was written.
suggested_refs: The October 1926 PCd'I Political Bureau letter to the Soviet party, and Togliatti's reply
sources: Marxists Internet Archive, letter to Togliatti, October 1926

stops.name: Rome, the arrest
stops.date_confidence: attested with a minor unresolved variance: the IGS chronology gives 8 November 1926, English Wikipedia's summary gives 9 November. Giuliano's birth in Moscow on 30 August 1926 and the fact that Gramsci never met him are attested by IGS and Wikipedia; the birth is recorded here rather than staged as a Moscow scene, since Gramsci was in Italy.
stops.campa: On the eighth of November, in the wave of arrests that follows the Bologna attempt on Mussolini's life, police take him from his rooms in Rome. He is a sitting deputy; the immunity is simply ignored. The following day the Chamber votes the mandates of the communist deputies forfeit and the Special Tribunal for the Defence of the State is created. Two months earlier Giulia had given birth in Moscow to their second son, Giuliano. Gramsci will never see him.
suggested_refs: The decree of 9 November 1926 establishing the Special Tribunal for the Defence of the State

stops.name: Rome, Regina Coeli
stops.date_confidence: attested; solitary confinement at Regina Coeli immediately after the arrest, and the administrative sentence of five years' confino on 18 November 1926, both from the IGS chronology. Coordinates are the prison's own published position. Tatiana Schucht was Gramsci's sister-in-law, Giulia's sister, and is described as such here to correct a common error.
stops.campa: He is held in solitary confinement at Regina Coeli, in Trastevere under the Janiculum. On the eighteenth of November a police commission sentences him administratively to five years of confino, internal exile, without a trial and without a charge that would need proving. He begins the correspondence that will run for the rest of his life, mostly with Giulia's sister Tatiana Schucht, who has stayed in Italy and who will become his link to everything outside: books, money, doctors, and eventually the notebooks themselves.
suggested_refs: The administrative confino order of 18 November 1926

stops.name: Ustica, the island school
stops.date_confidence: attested; arrival on Ustica 7 December 1926 after transport via Naples and Palermo, and the internees' school, both from the IGS chronology. The transit through the Ucciardone prison at Palermo is standard chronology but its date and duration are attested nowhere reached. The count of internees and the forty-four days are computed or standard rather than fetched.
stops.campa: Moved south in chains by way of Naples and the Ucciardone prison at Palermo, he lands on Ustica on the seventh of December, a volcanic island of a few hundred inhabitants holding several hundred political internees. The confinement is loose: the internees walk the island, cook together, and organize a school among themselves, in which Gramsci teaches history and geography. The regime then decides to try him after all, and on the seventh of February a new warrant pulls him off the island. He has been there forty-four days.
suggested_refs: The internees' school on Ustica, winter 1926-27

stops.name: Milan, San Vittore
stops.date_confidence: attested; arrival 7 February 1927 and interrogations by the investigating magistrate Enrico Macis from 9 February, per the IGS chronology. English Wikipedia lists Gramsci among San Vittore's inmates but gives no dates. The quotation is verbatim from the letter of 2 January 1928, written from this prison.
stops.campa: He arrives at San Vittore in Milan on the seventh of February and is held sixteen months awaiting trial, interrogated repeatedly by the investigating magistrate Enrico Macis. He petitions again and again for permission to read and write systematically in the cell. What he can send out is letters, and the letters begin to do the work the notebooks will do later, a recollection turning in mid-paragraph into an observation about how a trade marks the man who follows it. From outside, Tatiana Schucht and the economist Piero Sraffa work to get books past the censor to him.
stops.quote: I was completely unable to separate the image of the little poodle from his owner or from his profession.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Gramsci to Tatiana Schucht, 2 January 1928, Marxists Internet Archive translation
suggested_refs: The San Vittore letters to Tatiana Schucht, 1927-1928
sources: Marxists Internet Archive, letter of 2 January 1928

stops.name: Rome, the Special Tribunal
stops.date_confidence: trial dates and sentence attested by the IGS chronology, 28 May to 4 June 1928, twenty-two defendants, twenty years four months and five days; Britannica gives 'May 1928' for the sentence, a variance left standing. The quotation is trial tradition, not a documented transcript line: no stenographic record was located, sources render the wording differently, and no source reached attributes it to any named prosecutor. The wording used is the one given by English Wikipedia and by Joseph A. Buttigieg's translation.
stops.campa: He is tried in Rome with twenty-one other leaders of the Communist Party of Italy before the Special Tribunal, from the twenty-eighth of May to the fourth of June. The charges are conspiracy, incitement to civil war, and propaganda against the state. The line the prosecutor is remembered for appears in no surviving transcript, and has been the epitaph of the trial for a century regardless. On the fourth of June the court sentences him to twenty years, four months and five days.
stops.quote: For twenty years we must stop this brain from functioning.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to the prosecutor at Gramsci's trial before the Special Tribunal, Rome, 1928; wording as given by English Wikipedia and by Joseph A. Buttigieg's translation. Tradition, not a documented transcript line.
suggested_refs: The proceedings of the Special Tribunal for the Defence of the State in the processone of May-June 1928

stops.name: Turi, prisoner 7047
stops.date_confidence: attested; arrival 19 July 1928, the prisoner number and the single cell under surveillance from the IGS chronology, the building's history from Italian Wikipedia. Coordinates corrected: the incoming research repeated a latitude of 40.7647 across every Turi entry, which lands about 17 km south of the town in open country.
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of July he is delivered to the house of detention at Turi, in the Apulian countryside south of Bari: a building begun in 1850 as a convent for the Poor Clares, never occupied by nuns, seized by the state after 1866 and turned into a prison around 1895. He is registered as prisoner 7047 and put in a cell of his own, watched. He will be here five years and four months, the longest he has lived anywhere since Sardinia. He is thirty-seven and has already lost most of his teeth.
suggested_refs: Gramsci's preserved cell at the Casa Circondariale di Turi, kept with its original furnishings

stops.name: Turi, the first notebook
stops.date_confidence: attested; the IGS chronology and Britannica both give 8 February 1929 for the 'Main Topics' list that opens the First Notebook. The count of sixteen topics and the censor-code substitutions are standard in the scholarship and were not verified against a manuscript this pass.
stops.campa: Permission to write in the cell comes through at the end of January. On the eighth of February he opens a school exercise book, rules a margin, and writes at the head of the first page a list titled Main Topics: sixteen of them, from the theory of history to Americanism, from the Italian intellectuals to popular literature. Everything he writes will pass under the eye of a prison censor, so Karl Marx becomes the founder of the philosophy of praxis, Lenin becomes Ilyich, and the substitutions hold for the whole eight years of the writing.
suggested_refs: The First Notebook of the Quaderni del carcere, opened 8 February 1929

stops.name: Turi, the discussions and the silence after
stops.date_confidence: the November 1930 discussions and their discontinuation after negative reactions are attested by the IGS chronology; the day is unknown. The account of the political rupture with his fellow prisoners over the Third Period line rests on later testimony and censored correspondence rather than a contemporaneous neutral record, and is scholarly consensus rather than documentary fact.
stops.campa: In November he starts organized discussions among the political prisoners on the role of intellectuals and on the demand for a constituent assembly. The Comintern has just turned to the line that calls social democrats social fascists and forbids alliance with them; Gramsci argues instead for preparing a democratic transition out of fascism, and his comrades in the cells report him for it. The discussions are dropped. Some of the prisoners stop speaking to him altogether. He goes on writing.
suggested_refs: The Third Period line of the Comintern, 1928-1934, and the charge of social fascism

stops.name: Turi, the notebooks
stops.date_confidence: the scope and method of the notebooks are attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia; the date is a midpoint of the Turi writing years and orders the segment rather than marking an event. The quotation is Notebook 3, section 34, written about 1930, in the Hoare and Nowell-Smith translation, Selections from the Prison Notebooks (1971), 275-76.
stops.campa: He writes in fragments and reorders them, copying earlier notes into later books, a first draft and a second and sometimes a third of the same paragraph. Without a library, without correspondence he can trust, he works out what he calls hegemony: that a ruling class governs not chiefly by force but by making its own view of the world into common sense, and that a class meaning to replace it must win that ground before it wins any other. There are thirty-three notebooks by the time he stops, and he never sees any of them bound or printed.
stops.quote: The crisis consists precisely in the fact that the old is dying and the new cannot be born; in this interregnum a great variety of morbid symptoms appear.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Gramsci, Quaderni del carcere, Notebook 3 section 34, c. 1930, trans. Quintin Hoare and Geoffrey Nowell Smith, Selections from the Prison Notebooks (1971), 275-76
suggested_refs: Valentino Gerratana's critical edition of the Quaderni del carcere, Einaudi, four volumes, 1975

stops.name: Turi, the sentence reduced
stops.date_confidence: attested; the commutation to twelve years and four months on 10 November 1932 is given by the IGS chronology and confirmed by Britannica. The August 1931 crisis is attested in the general chronology; the detail of blood is standard in the biographies and was not fetched. Romain Rolland and Henri Barbusse are named by IGS as organizers of the international campaign.
stops.campa: His teeth are gone, he cannot digest solid food, he loses consciousness in the cell. From August 1931 the collapses come closer together; Tatiana Schucht and Sraffa press the authorities and an international campaign gathers abroad, with Romain Rolland and Henri Barbusse among its organizers. On the tenth of November, in an amnesty marking the tenth year of the regime, the sentence is reduced to twelve years and four months. He is forty-one years old and cannot walk the length of the corridor.
suggested_refs: The international campaign for Gramsci's release, organized in part by Romain Rolland and Henri Barbusse

stops.name: Turi, the news from Ghilarza
stops.date_confidence: the death of Giuseppina Marcias at Ghilarza on 30 December 1932 is attested by the IGS chronology. The concealment of the news is standard in secondary accounts and was not confirmed against a primary source. When and from whom Gramsci learned the truth is not recorded anywhere reached, and the stop leaves that open rather than filling it.
stops.campa: Giuseppina Marcias dies at Ghilarza on the thirtieth of December, in the house on Corso Umberto I where she held the family together through her husband's prison years. The family in Sardinia agrees not to tell him, fearing what it would do to him in the state he is in, and his sister Teresina goes on writing letters in which their mother is merely unwell. He writes back asking after her health. When he learned the truth, and from whom, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Casa Museo Antonio Gramsci, Corso Umberto I 57, Ghilarza, the house where his mother died

stops.name: Turi, the gate opens for a stretcher
stops.date_confidence: attested; Umberto Arcangeli's examination of 20 March 1933 and its finding that transfer was necessary, and the departure from Turi on 19 November 1933, both from the IGS chronology.
stops.campa: On the twentieth of March the specialist Umberto Arcangeli, permitted in from outside, examines him and writes that Gramsci cannot survive continued detention under the present regime. The report is published abroad and the campaign for his release grows loud enough to become a foreign policy problem. On the nineteenth of November, after eight months of negotiation, he is carried out of Turi prison. He is not released; he is transferred, still a prisoner, with a police guard assigned to his bed.
suggested_refs: Umberto Arcangeli's medical report of 20 March 1933, circulated abroad

stops.name: Formia, the Cusumano clinic
stops.date_confidence: attested; arrival at the Cusumano clinic at Formia on 7 December 1933, still a prisoner under guard, from the IGS chronology and the Fondazione Gramsci. Coordinates are the town centre: the clinic's street address was not located by any source reached. The split of the notebooks into seventeen from Turi and twelve from Formia comes from Italian Wikipedia's account of the Gerratana edition.
stops.campa: He is brought on the seventh of December to Dr Cusumano's clinic at Formia, on the Tyrrhenian coast between Rome and Naples, and put in a room with a guard at the door and a bar on the window. He can see the sea. Tatiana Schucht moves to Formia to be near him. The writing does not resume as it was: the notebooks that came with him from Turi are added to, but the long systematic work is over, and the twelve books filled here are thinner and more repetitive than the seventeen filled in the cell.
suggested_refs: The twelve Formia notebooks, distinguished from the seventeen written at Turi in Gerratana's 1975 edition

stops.name: Formia, conditional liberty
stops.date_confidence: attested; conditional freedom granted 25 October 1934, with brief outings in the company of his brother Carlo, his sister-in-law Tatiana Schucht and the economist Piero Sraffa, per the IGS chronology. The refusal of permission to leave Italy is standard in the accounts of the release campaign.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of October he is granted conditional freedom: he may leave the clinic for short periods in the company of approved persons. He is not permitted to leave Italy, which is the one thing that might have saved him and the one thing the regime will not concede; the applications go in and come back refused. He goes out with his brother Carlo, with Tatiana Schucht, and with Piero Sraffa, who comes down from Cambridge. He walks a little on the seafront, watched the whole time.
suggested_refs: Piero Sraffa's correspondence and interventions on Gramsci's behalf from Cambridge

stops.name: Rome, the Quisisana
stops.date_confidence: attested; arrival at the Clinica Quisisana, Via Gian Giacomo Porro 5, on 24 August 1935, the clinic run by the Sisters of the Holy Cross, per the Fondazione Gramsci. Coordinates corrected to the surveyed position of the address, about 800 m from the pin given in the incoming research.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of August he is moved to the Quisisana clinic in Rome, in Via Gian Giacomo Porro, a private house of care run by the Sisters of the Holy Cross in the Parioli district. He has a room on the ground floor with a veranda. Arteriosclerosis, tuberculosis, hypertension, Pott's disease: the certificates list them together. He is forty-four. The notebooks stay in a trunk in Tatiana Schucht's keeping and he does not open them again. He asks for news of his sons.
suggested_refs: The Clinica Quisisana, Via Gian Giacomo Porro 5, Rome, run by the Sisters of the Holy Cross

stops.name: Rome, the letter to Julike
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter to Giuliano is dated 24 November 1936 in the Marxists Internet Archive text, from which the quotation is verbatim. Julike is Gramsci's own diminutive for his younger son. Delio's letters about geography are described in the same correspondence.
stops.campa: He writes to Giuliano in Moscow, a boy of ten he has never seen, and tells him his handwriting has improved and that he now writes like a big boy. The letters to the two sons are the plainest prose he ever produced: no politics, no theory, no code for the censor, only the questions a father asks who has nothing else to go on and no expectation of being answered soon. He has five months left. Delio writes back about geography. Giuliano sends drawings.
stops.quote_source: Antonio Gramsci to his son Giuliano, 24 November 1936, Marxists Internet Archive translation
suggested_refs: The prison letters to Delio and Giuliano Gramsci, 1936-1937
sources: Marxists Internet Archive, letter to Giuliano, 24 November 1936

stops.name: Rome, the twenty-seventh of April
stops.date_confidence: attested in detail by the Fondazione Gramsci: the 12:30 p.m. notification on 25 April that conditional liberty had ended and surveillance was suspended, the haemorrhage that evening, the worsening on the 26th, death early on the 27th. The IGS chronology and Britannica agree the sentence expired 21 April 1937. Tatiana Schucht was his sister-in-law, not his sister, a common error corrected here.
stops.campa: His sentence had formally expired on the twenty-first. At half past twelve on the twenty-fifth of April he is notified that the conditional liberty has ended and the police surveillance is withdrawn: after ten years and five months he is, in law, a free man. That evening a cerebral haemorrhage paralyses his left side. He worsens through the twenty-sixth and dies in the early hours of the twenty-seventh of April, forty-six years old. Tatiana Schucht is at the bedside. His brother Carlo arrives after.
suggested_refs: The former Clinica Quisisana, Rome, subject of a 2023 appeal by more than a thousand scholars for a commemorative plaque

stops.name: Rome, the common grave at Verano
stops.date_confidence: attested; the IGS chronology states that the funeral was held under police surveillance and that the ashes were buried in a common grave at the Verano cemetery. English Wikipedia omits the Verano burial entirely and describes interment at the Protestant cemetery directly, a discrepancy left standing. Coordinates corrected to the cemetery's own published position, about a kilometre from the pin in the incoming research.
stops.campa: The funeral is held on the twenty-eighth of April under police surveillance, the mourners few and counted at the gate. The body is cremated and the ashes are put into a common grave at the Campo Verano, the municipal cemetery beside San Lorenzo fuori le Mura. There is no stone and no inscription. Which of the family got to Rome in time for it, the chronology does not say. Of the twenty years, four months and five days the Special Tribunal gave him, he had served ten years, five months and nineteen days.
suggested_refs: The common-grave section of the Cimitero del Verano, Rome, where the ashes lay from 1937 to 1938

stops.name: Rome, the Non-Catholic Cemetery
stops.date_confidence: attested to late 1938 by the IGS chronology; the day is unknown and 1 December orders the segment. Coordinates are the cemetery's published position; the plot within the grounds is not specified by any source reached. The publication history in the refs is later than the file's own clock and is offered as reference apparatus, not as scene.
stops.campa: In late 1938 the ashes are lifted from the common grave and carried across Rome to the Cimitero Acattolico at Testaccio, the burial ground for non-Catholics under the Aurelian wall beside the pyramid of Cestius, where Keats and Shelley lie. The notebooks come out of Moscow after the war and are printed in Turin, and the grave becomes a place people travel to on purpose. Ghilarza will make a museum of the house on Corso Umberto I. The urn goes under a low stone with the name, the dates, and nothing else.
suggested_refs: Pier Paolo Pasolini, 'Le ceneri di Gramsci', written 1954, published 1957, staged at this grave and winner of the Viareggio Prize
